questions.question: What are derived query methods in Spring Data JPA?
questions.title: Derived Query Methods in Spring Data JPA — Name-Based Query Generation
questions.direct_answer: **Derived query methods** let Spring Data JPA generate the query from the **method name**. Declaring `findByLastName(String name)` produces `WHERE last_name = ?` — no SQL, no `@Query`. Spring **parses the name at startup** into a query, so a typo or unknown field fails the application boot (fast feedback), not at runtime.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand name-based query generation and that names are validated at startup against entity fields
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing @Query JPQL for simple conditions derived methods already handle, or omitting @Transactional on deleteBy
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention startup-time parsing/validation and the keyword grammar (And, Or, GreaterThan, Between, OrderBy, Top)

sections.title: Auto-Generated Queries from Method Names
sections.content:
**Derived query methods** are Spring Data JPA's headline productivity feature: you declare a method signature in a repository interface following a naming grammar, and Spring generates the query implementation **at application startup** — no `@Query`, no SQL, no implementation class.

Spring reads `findByLastNameAndAge(String lastName, int age)` and turns it into `WHERE last_name = ? AND age = ?`. Each keyword maps to a SQL fragment: `findBy` → SELECT, `And`/`Or` → boolean logic, `Between`/`GreaterThan`/`In` → operators, `OrderBy` → sorting. If the name breaks the grammar or references an unknown field, the app **fails fast at boot** with a `PropertyReferenceException` — a clear, early error instead of a production surprise.

sections.title: Derived Method Grammar at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Subject keyword|~What it does|findBy / getBy / readBy = SELECT|countBy = COUNT|existsBy = EXISTS, deleteBy = DELETE
blue|Conditions|~The WHERE clause|And / Or|GreaterThan, LessThan, Between, In|IsNull, Containing
emerald|Modifiers|~Shape the result|OrderBy...Asc/Desc|Top / First N|IgnoreCase, Distinct
violet|Validation|~Fail fast|parsed at startup|fields matched to entity|typo = boot error, not runtime

sections.title: A Repository Full of Derived Methods
sections.content:
```java
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {

    List<User> findByLastName(String lastName);                 // WHERE last_name = ?

    Optional<User> findByEmailAndStatus(String email, String status); // AND

    List<User> findByAgeGreaterThanOrderByCreatedAtDesc(int age);     // > ? ORDER BY ... DESC

    List<User> findByCreatedAtBetween(LocalDateTime start, LocalDateTime end); // BETWEEN

    long countByDepartment(String department);                 // COUNT(*)

    boolean existsByEmail(String email);                        // EXISTS

    @Transactional
    void deleteByStatus(String status);                        // DELETE — needs a transaction
}
```

sections.title: Wrong — Misspelled Property in the Method Name
Right — Property Names Match the Entity Fields
sections.content:
```java
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
    List<User> findByLastName(String lastName);   // matches User.lastName
    List<User> findByEmail(String email);         // matches User.email
}
```
Spring validates every property against the entity at startup, so a typo fails the boot, not production.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Field-name typos** — `findByNameLastName` instead of `findByLastName`; the property must match the entity field, else `PropertyReferenceException` at startup.
- **`deleteBy` without `@Transactional`** — throws `TransactionRequiredException` at runtime; writes need a transaction.
- **Overusing derived methods** — `findByFirstNameAndLastNameAndAgeAndDepartmentAndStatus` is unreadable; switch to `@Query` past ~3 conditions.
- **Reaching for `@Query` too early** — for simple `findByEmail`, a derived method is cleaner.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Method name → query** — Spring parses it at **startup** and generates the implementation.
- **Subject keywords**: `findBy`, `countBy`, `existsBy`, `deleteBy`.
- **Conditions/operators**: `And`, `Or`, `GreaterThan`, `Between`, `In`, `IsNull`, `Containing`.
- **Result shaping**: `OrderBy...Asc/Desc`, `Top`/`First`, `IgnoreCase`, `Distinct`.
- **`deleteBy` needs `@Transactional`**; typos fail at boot, not at runtime.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Derived query methods are a Spring Data JPA feature where I just write a method signature in my repository interface and Spring generates the query by reading the method name. For example, if I write findByLastName with a String parameter, Spring builds a select with a where clause on the last name field. I don't write any SQL or annotations. This works because Spring parses the method name at application startup. It breaks the name into parts — findBy means it's a select, LastName maps to the last name field on my entity, and the parameter becomes a where condition. I can combine conditions with And or Or, like findByEmailAndStatus. There are operator keywords too, like findByAgeGreaterThan, and result shapers like OrderBy, Top, and IgnoreCase. The mistake Learners make is writing a custom Query annotation for simple lookups that a derived method handles perfectly. Another gotcha is delete methods: if I write deleteByStatus I have to add Transactional, or it throws at runtime. Something interviewers like to hear is that if my method name doesn't follow the grammar or references a field that doesn't exist, the application fails at startup with a clear error, which is much better than discovering it in production. So derived methods keep repositories clean and readable, and when the names get long with many conditions, that's the signal to switch to a Query annotation with JPQL.

questions.question: What is the findBy...Containing and findBy...Like in Spring Data JPA?
questions.title: Containing, Like, StartingWith — String Matching in Spring Data JPA
questions.direct_answer: Spring Data JPA supports keywords such as Containing, StartingWith, EndingWith, and Like. Containing/StartingWith/EndingWith augment the bound pattern as documented, while Like expects the caller's SQL LIKE pattern. IgnoreCase requests case-insensitive comparison. A leading wildcard usually prevents a normal B-tree prefix seek, but expression, full-text, or trigram indexes can change the plan.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know which keywords add wildcards automatically and the index/performance impact of a leading %
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Passing %text% to Containing (double wildcards) or omitting % with Like and getting an exact match
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention IgnoreCase for user search and that leading % forces a full scan (StartingWith is index-friendly)

sections.title: Derived String Matching Keywords
sections.content:
Case sensitivity depends on the database, collation, column type, and generated expression. IgnoreCase may use LOWER on both sides; an ordinary index may then need a matching functional index to help.

Wildcard characters in user input need an explicit product decision: are % and _ literal search text or pattern syntax? Escape them when literal matching is intended. For advanced ranking, language stemming, or large contains search, use the database's full-text facilities rather than stretching a derived method.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Containing searches for a value within text; StartingWith and EndingWith anchor one side.
Like accepts pattern wildcard characters from the supplied value.
IgnoreCase behavior is rendered through provider/database expressions and collation rules.
Inspect generated SQL and the plan for large text searches.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: findByNameStartingWith("Ann") commonly produces a prefix LIKE pattern, while findByNameContaining("ann") produces a contains pattern. findByNameLike("Ann%") lets the caller supply the pattern. These methods bind the value; do not concatenate it into @Query text. A normal B-tree can often support a compatible prefix pattern, while contains search may need a database-specific text index.

sections.title: String Matchers at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Containing|~Both wildcards auto|LIKE %text%|pass raw text|general search box
blue|StartingWith|~Trailing wildcard|LIKE text%|index-friendly|autocomplete / prefixes
emerald|EndingWith|~Leading wildcard|LIKE %text|full scan risk|suffix / domain match
violet|Like|~You add wildcards|pattern as-is|_ matches one char|full control
rose|IgnoreCase|~Case-insensitive|LOWER() both sides|append to any matcher|user-facing search

sections.title: Wrong — Double Wildcards and Missing Wildcards
Right — Let Containing Add Wildcards; Add Them Yourself for Like
sections.content:
```java
public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {
    List<Product> findByNameContainingIgnoreCase(String keyword); // pass raw "phone"
    List<Product> findByNameStartingWith(String prefix);          // "Apple" → 'Apple%'
    List<Product> findByNameLike(String pattern);                 // you pass "%phone%"
}

// usage
repo.findByNameContainingIgnoreCase("phone"); // LOWER(name) LIKE LOWER('%phone%')
repo.findByNameLike("%phone%");               // you supply the wildcards
```
For user-facing search always use `IgnoreCase`; prefer `StartingWith` on large tables for index use.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Adding `%` to `Containing`** — `findByNameContaining("%phone%")` becomes `LIKE '%%phone%%'`; pass raw text.
- **Forgetting `%` with `Like`** — `findByNameLike("john")` is an exact match; you must pass `%john%`.
- **Skipping `IgnoreCase`** — "iPhone" won't match "iphone"; users expect case-insensitive search.
- **Ignoring performance** — `Containing` on a 10M-row table does a full scan because the leading `%` defeats indexes.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: Use **derived methods** for simple conditions (1-3 fields) where the name stays readable. Switch to **`@Query`** when the name exceeds ~60-70 chars, or you need **JOIN, GROUP BY, aggregates (COUNT/SUM/AVG), subqueries, or DB-specific SQL** — things derived methods simply can't express. Readability and capability are the deciding factors.

questions.question: How do you use findBy...In() and findBy...Between() in Spring Data?
questions.title: findByIn and findByBetween in Spring Data JPA — Collection and Range Queries
questions.direct_answer: findByStatusIn(Collection<Status>) creates an IN predicate, while findByAgeBetween(min, max) creates an inclusive BETWEEN predicate. Empty collection behavior should not be described as universally invalid SQL: repository query generation and database/provider handling differ. Decide explicitly whether an empty input should return an empty result, skip the filter, or be rejected.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you reach for In/Between instead of custom @Query for multi-value and range filters
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing In exists (writing @Query for IN), or passing an empty list and breaking the SQL
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention findByIdIn for bulk fetch, BETWEEN being inclusive, and IN-clause size limits

sections.title: Derived IN and BETWEEN Queries
sections.content:
A date example shows the boundary issue. BETWEEN 2026-09-01 00:00 and 2026-09-30 00:00 does not include the rest of September 30. A half-open range from September 1 inclusive to October 1 exclusive avoids precision assumptions.

For IN, a few known statuses are straightforward. Thousands of IDs may exceed a database-specific parameter limit or create an expensive plan. Split batches only after considering transaction consistency, or use a temporary table, join, or another database-specific technique when the workload justifies it.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: In accepts a Collection, array, or varargs for membership matching.
Between includes both lower and upper endpoints.
Empty inputs need an application contract; do not rely on one database's generated SQL behavior.
Large lists may hit vendor limits or produce poor plans; batch or redesign when measured.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Spring Data parses In and Between as supported query keywords. findByStatusIn(statuses) binds a collection to a membership predicate. findByCreatedAtBetween(start, end) includes both boundaries, which makes a half-open time range often clearer for timestamps: GreaterThanEqual(start) and LessThan(end). An empty collection is not a portable 'invalid SQL' rule. Derived queries, manually written @Query methods, Hibernate versions, and databases can handle it differently. Validate the input and make the desired result explicit.

sections.title: In and Between at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|In|~Multiple values|WHERE status IN (...)|works with List/Set|findByIdIn = bulk fetch
blue|Between|~A range|WHERE age BETWEEN a AND b|inclusive both ends|numbers, dates, Comparable
emerald|Exclusive range|~Need open bounds|GreaterThan + LessThan|combine with And|when BETWEEN won't do
violet|Limits|~Watch out|empty list = invalid SQL|Oracle caps IN at 1000|batch large lists

sections.title: Wrong — Custom @Query for IN, and an Unguarded Empty List
Right — Derived In/Between with an Empty-List Guard
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing `In` exists** — writing a custom `@Query` IN clause when `findByStatusIn` does it.
- **Empty collection** — `findByStatusIn(List.of())` → `IN ()`, invalid SQL; guard or validate.
- **Wrong `Between` boundaries** — `BETWEEN 10 AND 20` includes both 10 and 20; use `GreaterThan`/`LessThan` for exclusive ranges.
- **Timezone bugs** — using `LocalDateTime.now()` in date ranges without timezone care causes off-by-hours errors.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: Use **derived methods** for simple conditions (1-3 fields) where the name stays readable. Switch to **`@Query`** when the name exceeds ~60-70 chars, or you need **JOIN, GROUP BY, aggregates (COUNT/SUM/AVG), subqueries, or DB-specific SQL** — things derived methods simply can't express. Readability and capability are the deciding factors.

questions.question: How do you limit query results with Top and First in Spring Data JPA?
questions.title: findTop and findFirst in Spring Data JPA — Limiting Query Results
questions.direct_answer: Top and First in a Spring Data method name limit the maximum number of returned rows. The JPA provider translates that limit into database-specific SQL, not necessarily the literal LIMIT keyword. Add a deterministic sort when 'first' or 'top' has business meaning; without ordering, which matching row is returned is not guaranteed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you limit at the database level and know Top/First are synonyms requiring OrderBy to be meaningful
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling findAll() then Stream.limit() — loads everything into memory instead of using SQL LIMIT
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note findFirst equals findTop1, and combining Top with OrderBy gives efficient 'latest N' queries

sections.title: Limiting Derived Query Results
Quick revision
content: findFirst is the one-result form; findTop3 limits to three.
Use OrderBy in the name or pass Sort/Pageable for deterministic selection.
Limiting happens in the database through provider/dialect support.
SQL text may use LIMIT, FETCH FIRST, TOP, or another dialect form.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A method such as findTop3ByStatusOrderByCreatedAtDesc asks for at most three matching rows, sorted newest first. findFirstByEmail can return Optional<User> when at most one result is expected. The limiting expression is part of the repository query model and Hibernate renders the form understood by the configured database. Without ORDER BY, relational results have no guaranteed order, so 'first' only means some matching row. Include a unique tie-breaker such as id when stable ordering matters.

sections.title: Top / First at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|findFirst / findTop1|~Single row|returns Optional<T>|same thing|most-recent / highest
blue|findTopN|~N rows|returns List<T>|SQL LIMIT N|top 5, top 10, ...
emerald|+ OrderBy|~Makes it meaningful|...OrderByCreatedAtDesc|latest / oldest / highest|required for sense
violet|vs Stream.limit|~Where it happens|LIMIT at the DB|not load-all-then-trim|memory + speed win

sections.title: Wrong — Load Everything, Limit in Java
sections.content:
```java
// Loads ALL matching rows into memory, then throws most away
List<Order> recent = orderRepository.findAll().stream()
        .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Order::getCreatedAt).reversed())
        .limit(5)
        .toList();
```

sections.title: Right — LIMIT at the Database with Top/First
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`findAll()` + `Stream.limit()`** — loads thousands of rows to keep 5; use `Top`/`First`.
- **Forgetting `OrderBy`** — `findTop10ByStatus(...)` returns 10 arbitrary rows, not the 10 you want.
- **Confusing First and Top** — both limit; `findFirst` = `findTop1`, just naming style.
- **Expecting null** — `findTopN` returns a `List` (possibly empty); `findFirst` returns `Optional`.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: Use **derived methods** for simple conditions (1-3 fields) where the name stays readable. Switch to **`@Query`** when the name exceeds ~60-70 chars, or you need **JOIN, GROUP BY, aggregates (COUNT/SUM/AVG), subqueries, or DB-specific SQL** — things derived methods simply can't express. Readability and capability are the deciding factors.

questions.question: How do you write a custom JPQL query with @Query in Spring Data JPA?
questions.title: @Query Annotation in Spring Data JPA — JPQL and Native SQL
questions.direct_answer: @Query attaches a JPQL query or, with nativeQuery=true, database SQL to a repository method. JPQL uses entity names and mapped attributes; native SQL uses table/column names and database syntax. Use it when a derived method would be unclear or cannot express the required shape. There is no useful universal method-name character limit.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can write JPQL/native queries and know the @Modifying + @Transactional requirement for writes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting @Modifying/@Transactional on UPDATE/DELETE, or using table names in JPQL
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show JOIN FETCH for N+1, named vs positional params, and when nativeQuery=true is justified

sections.title: Custom Repository Queries with @Query
sections.content:
Derived methods can traverse mapped properties and express many comparisons, ranges, membership tests, ordering, and limits. @Query becomes clearer for projections, explicit joins/fetches, aggregation, subqueries supported by the query language, or carefully isolated native features. Pagination plus collection fetch joins needs special care because multiplied rows can make page results/counting incorrect or inefficient.

**Example.** select o from Order o where o.status=:status is JPQL over an entity field, while select * from orders where status=:status is native table SQL.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Bind values with named or positional parameters; do not concatenate input.
Use @Modifying for bulk UPDATE and DELETE repository queries.
Run modifying queries within an appropriate transaction.
A fetch join is one fetch-plan tool, not a guarantee of the fastest or single-statement solution in every case.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: For example, @Query("select o from Order o where o.status=:status order by o.createdAt desc") List<Order> findRecent(@Param("status") Status status) expresses a readable JPQL query. A bulk update such as update Order o set o.status=:next where o.status=:old needs @Modifying and a transaction; it also bypasses ordinary per-entity dirty checking and can leave managed instances stale.

sections.title: @Query Options at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|JPQL|~Entity-level|FROM User u (class)|u.email (field)|portable, validated
blue|Native|~nativeQuery = true|raw table SQL|DB functions (INTERVAL)|not portable
emerald|Params|~Binding|:name + @Param (named)|?1 (positional)|named preferred
violet|Writes|~UPDATE/DELETE|need @Modifying|need @Transactional|else exception
cyan|JOIN FETCH|~N+1 fix|load relation in one query|avoid lazy loops|performance

sections.title: Wrong — UPDATE Without @Modifying / Table Name in JPQL
Right — JPQL, JOIN FETCH, and a Proper @Modifying Update
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Missing `@Modifying`** on UPDATE/DELETE — Hibernate assumes a read query and throws.
- **No `@Transactional`** — even with `@Modifying`, writes need a transaction.
- **Table names in JPQL** — `FROM orders` fails; use the entity `FROM Order`.
- **Native query and entity state** — native results aren't managed; changes won't auto-flush unless you `save()`.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: Use **derived methods** for simple conditions (1-3 fields) where the name stays readable. Switch to **`@Query`** when the name exceeds ~60-70 chars, or you need **JOIN, GROUP BY, aggregates (COUNT/SUM/AVG), subqueries, or DB-specific SQL** — things derived methods simply can't express. Readability and capability are the deciding factors.

questions.question: When should you use @Query instead of a derived query method?
questions.title: @Query vs Derived Methods — Choosing the Right Approach
questions.direct_answer: Use a derived method when its supported keywords express the query clearly. Use @Query when the name becomes hard to read or when explicit JPQL/native SQL is needed for projections, complex joins, aggregation, subqueries, or provider/database features. There is no meaningful character-count cutoff, and derived methods can traverse relationships and express more than only one to three fields.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical judgment on the readability/capability trade-off between derived methods and @Query
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Cramming 5-6 conditions into a derived method name instead of a clear @Query, or thinking derived methods can do JOIN/GROUP BY
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give concrete thresholds (3 conditions, ~70 chars) and note aggregates/joins force @Query

sections.title: Choosing a Derived Method or @Query
sections.content:
A long name such as findTop20ByStatusAndCustomerRegionAndCreatedAtBetweenOrderByCreatedAtDesc may still be mechanically valid, yet it hides the query shape. Rewriting it as named JPQL can make joins and projection explicit. Conversely, a one-line findByExternalId does not become better because it is written as @Query.

Whichever form is chosen, keep parameter binding, verify empty and null behavior, and inspect the plan for performance-sensitive queries. The query authoring style does not remove the need for indexes or correct transaction boundaries.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Derived query: concise, supported condition whose method name remains clear.
@Query: explicit JPQL or native SQL when the query shape needs to be seen.
Do not use a made-up 60- or 70-character rule.
Test behavior and generated SQL for important queries regardless of authoring style.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
findByEmailIgnoreCase is easier to understand as a derived method than as a separate JPQL string. A report with joins, grouped totals, and a DTO projection is clearer as @Query or a custom repository. Derived query keywords support nested properties, sorting, limiting, count, delete, and many predicates, so they are not restricted to three fields. The decision is readability and capability. Native SQL trades portability for database-specific features; JPQL stays in the entity model but still needs tests for generated SQL and performance.

For example, findByStatusOrderByCreatedAtDesc is clear for a simple lookup. A report joining orders and customers with projections and grouped totals is clearer as @Query or a custom repository implementation.

sections.title: Pick the Right Tool at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Derived method|~Simple lookups|1-3 conditions|self-documenting|no SQL needed
blue|@Query (JPQL)|~Complex but portable|joins, aggregates|named params|when names get long
emerald|@Query (native)|~DB-specific|JSONB, window fns|nativeQuery = true|last resort
violet|Readability rule|~The threshold|~60-70 char name|>3 conditions|switch to @Query

sections.title: Derived Methods vs @Query
sections.content:
| Need | Derived method | @Query |
|---|---|---|
| 1-3 simple conditions | Best fit | Overkill |
| 4+ conditions / long name | Unreadable | Best fit |
| JOIN across entities | Not possible | Required |
| GROUP BY / COUNT / SUM | Not possible | Required |
| Subqueries | Not possible | Required |
| DB-specific SQL | Not possible | `nativeQuery = true` |

Rule: more than a `WHERE` with AND/OR → use `@Query`.

sections.title: Wrong — A Six-Condition Derived Method Name
Right — Clear @Query (and an Aggregate Derived Methods Can't Do)
When to Use Each
sections.content: Use **derived methods** for simple, readable lookups (1-3 conditions): `findByEmail`, `findByStatus`. Use **`@Query` with JPQL** when the name would balloon, when you need `JOIN`/`JOIN FETCH`, projections/DTOs, or aggregates like `COUNT`/`AVG`/`GROUP BY`. Use **`@Query(nativeQuery = true)`** for DB-specific features (PostgreSQL JSONB, full-text search) or heavy reporting SQL. The honest test: if you can't read the query at a glance, rewrite it as `@Query`.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Choosing between findByEmailAndStatus and a JPQL @Query
speakable_v2.hook: A seventy-character method name screams for a Query annotation. Joins and grouping leave you no choice anyway.

groups.heading: Derived methods
groups.text: The method name defines the query. findByEmailAndStatus reads as plain English and needs no SQL.

groups.heading: Query annotation
groups.text: You write JPQL or native SQL by hand. It handles joins, grouping, and anything a name can't express.

values: Best for one to three conditions.
Best for long or complex queries.
Handles joins, group by, and counts.

beats.text: Pick a derived method for simple, readable lookups of one to three fields. Switch to the Query annotation once the name gets long. Anything with a join or a group by forces it too.

Take a six-condition filter on products. As a derived method the name turns into an unreadable paragraph. Important: aggregates like average order per customer have no derived form, so JPQL stays the only option.

speakable_v2.cap: So derived methods win for simple reads, and the Query annotation takes over once things get complex.
